B1:
Cause: Touched fires once for every body part that touches the part (feet, legs, torso), and several times as contacts flicker. Several events are queued in the same frame before part:Destroy() takes effect, so each one runs the handler and adds 10 coins. Accessories also make hit.Parent wrong sometimes.
Fix: add a guard (debounce) and disconnect.
```lua
local part = script.Parent
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local collected = false
local conn
conn = part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    if collected then return end
    local plr = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
    if not plr then return end
    collected = true
    conn:Disconnect()
    plr.leaderstats.Coins.Value += 10
    part:Destroy()
end)
```
Set the flag before any yield. For per-player pickups, use a table keyed by player.
B2:
With StreamingEnabled, the client only has instances near the player. Distant buildings and their doors aren't streamed in yet, so indexing workspace.Map.Buildings.Hotel.Door throws "not a valid member". The parts can also stream out later, so the reference becomes invalid.
Fixes:
1. Make the model persistent or atomic: set Hotel (or the Door model) ModelStreamingMode = Persistent, so it is always present on clients (use sparingly). Or set Atomic and wait for it with WaitForChild.
2. Don't assume it exists. Use CollectionService tags: tag doors "Door", then use GetInstanceAddedSignal("Door") and GetTagged to connect when a door streams in, and clean up on GetInstanceRemovedSignal. This works for every door, near or far. (Equivalent: WaitForChild with a timeout, or ChildAdded handling, but tags are the standard fix.)
Better still, do door-touch logic on the server, where everything exists, and use the client only for visuals. Also use player:RequestStreamAroundAsync if you need an area loaded before teleporting the player there.
B3:
Bugs:
1. It always returns PurchaseGranted, even if pcall failed. So when the save errors, the receipt is closed and the player is charged but gets nothing.
2. It ignores a player who isn't present. If plr is nil, plr.UserId errors inside the pcall, so nothing is saved, but it still returns Granted.
3. There is no idempotency. Roblox retries receipts (timeout, rejoin, server crash after the save but before the return), and each retry adds 100 again, giving double coins. There is no PurchaseId record.
4. GetAsync + SetAsync is a non-atomic read-modify-write. Another server or autosave can race and overwrite.
5. It probably doesn't update the in-memory session data, so the next autosave overwrites the purchase.
Corrected behaviour: look up the player, and return NotProcessedYet if they are absent. In one UpdateAsync on the player's key, if receipts[PurchaseId] already exists, change nothing; otherwise add 100 coins and record the PurchaseId. Return Granted only if pcall succeeded; on any error, return NotProcessedYet. Then update the live session or leaderstats. Check ProductId, and keep a single ProcessReceipt assignment.
B4:
1. Metatables are not sent over remotes. Tables are serialized by value, so the client gets {Name="Rifle", Ammo=30} with no metatable, Weapon.__index is gone and Fire is nil. Functions can't be sent either. Fix: send plain data (an id plus state), and on the client rebuild the object with a shared class module in ReplicatedStorage: `local w = setmetatable(data, require(RS.Weapon))` or `Weapon.new(data)`.
2. Instance arguments are sent as references and only resolve if the instance is replicated to that client. ServerStorage never replicates, so the client receives nil. (The same happens with instances that aren't streamed in yet.) Fix: put Muzzle in ReplicatedStorage, or in workspace under the weapon, or send an identifier or the data the client needs (CFrame, name) instead of the instance.
Also keep in mind: mixed and sparse tables and non-string keys get mangled, and the client must not be trusted with authoritative weapon state like Ammo.
B5:
workspace:Raycast's second argument is the direction and length vector, not just a direction. dir is a unit vector, so the ray is only 1 stud long and only hits things touching the barrel. Fix: scale it to the range or the distance, and add RaycastParams to ignore the shooter.
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local offset = target - origin
local MAX = 300
local dir = offset.Unit * math.min(offset.Magnitude + 1, MAX) -- or offset.Unit * MAX
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
Also guard against a zero-length offset (target == origin gives a NaN Unit vector).
B6:
When the last player leaves (or the server is shut down), the server closes. PlayerRemoving fires, but the server can be torn down before the yielding SetAsync finishes. Also, on shutdown, PlayerRemoving handlers may not complete. So the save is lost.
Standard fix: use game:BindToClose to save every remaining player and wait until all saves finish (you get about 30 seconds). Run saves in parallel with task.spawn and wait for completion. Make the PlayerRemoving and BindToClose saves share one save function with a per-player "saving/saved" guard, so they don't double-write. Use UpdateAsync with pcall and retries, and also autosave periodically.
```lua
game:BindToClose(function()
    if game:GetService("RunService"):IsStudio() then end -- still save, or skip for speed
    local pending = 0
    for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
        pending += 1
        task.spawn(function() savePlayer(p, true); pending -= 1 end)
    end
    while pending > 0 do task.wait() end
end)
```
A session-locking library (ProfileStore) handles this for you.

```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local UseAbility = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.UseAbility
local COOLDOWN = 2
local lastUse: {[Player]: number} = {}

UseAbility.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, abilityId)
    if typeof(abilityId) ~= "string" then return end
    local now = os.clock()
    local last = lastUse[player]
    if last and now - last < COOLDOWN then return end -- silently ignore spam
    lastUse[player] = now
    local char = player.Character
    local hum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not hum or hum.Health <= 0 then return end
    performAbility(player, abilityId) -- server-side effect
end)

Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
    lastUse[player] = nil -- no leak
end)
```
The cooldown is server-authoritative (os.clock), and the timestamp is set before any yield. Don't fire anything back for rejected spam. Per-ability cooldowns can use a nested table, also cleared on PlayerRemoving.

```lua
local MPS = game:GetService("MarketplaceService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local DSS = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DSS:GetDataStore("PlayerData")
local GEMS100 = 123456

local function grant(data, receipt)
    if receipt.ProductId == GEMS100 then data.Gems = (data.Gems or 0) + 100 return true end
    return false
end

MPS.ProcessReceipt = function(receipt)
    local player = Players:GetPlayerByUserId(receipt.PlayerId)
    if not player then return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end

    local granted = false
    local ok, err = pcall(function()
        store:UpdateAsync("u_" .. receipt.PlayerId, function(data)
            data = data or {Gems = 0, Receipts = {}}
            data.Receipts = data.Receipts or {}
            if data.Receipts[receipt.PurchaseId] then granted = true return nil end
            if not grant(data, receipt) then return nil end
            data.Receipts[receipt.PurchaseId] = os.time()
            granted = true -- set per attempt; last run wins
            return data
        end)
    end)
    if not ok or not granted then
        warn("Receipt failed", err)
        return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet
    end
    -- reflect in live session/leaderstats
    local gems = player:FindFirstChild("leaderstats") and player.leaderstats:FindFirstChild("Gems")
    if gems then gems.Value += 100 end
    return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
end
```

Assign it once. Prune old receipt ids (keep the last ~50). If you use session-locked data (ProfileStore), grant into the profile and save it instead of writing the store directly, so an autosave can't overwrite the grant.

```lua
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local info = TweenInfo.new(0.4, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)
local SHOWN = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0)
local HIDDEN = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 1.5, 0)
menu.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5)
local current

local function open()
    if current then current:Cancel() end
    menu.Position = HIDDEN
    menu.Visible = true
    current = TweenService:Create(menu, info, {Position = SHOWN})
    current:Play()
end

local function close()
    if current then current:Cancel() end
    local t = TweenService:Create(menu, info, {Position = HIDDEN})
    current = t
    t.Completed:Connect(function(state)
        if state == Enum.PlaybackState.Completed and current == t then
            menu.Visible = false
        end
    end)
    t:Play()
end
```
Hiding only on a Completed state (and only if this is still the current tween) prevents a quick reopen from being hidden by a stale close tween.

```lua
local MAX_RANGE, DAMAGE = 200, 20

local function shoot(player: Player, targetPos: Vector3)
    if typeof(targetPos) ~= "Vector3" or targetPos ~= targetPos then return end
    local char = player.Character
    local head = char and char:FindFirstChild("Head")
    local hum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not head or not hum or hum.Health <= 0 then return end

    end
end
```

```lua
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local TAG = "KillBrick"
local conns: {[BasePart]: RBXScriptConnection} = {}

local function onAdded(part)

CollectionService:GetInstanceRemovedSignal(TAG):Connect(onRemoved)
```

B13:
(a) Buying is client to server. Use a RemoteFunction (client InvokeServer, server OnServerInvoke returns success/reason) or a RemoteEvent. The client sends only the intent (itemId). The server holds the authoritative coin balance (session data/leaderstats) and the price catalogue. It validates the item, price and funds, deducts the coins, grants the sword, and saves.
(b) Updating the counter is server to client. Either let replication do it (a leaderstats IntValue or a player Attribute the client listens to with GetPropertyChangedSignal/Changed), or FireClient a RemoteEvent with the new balance. The client UI only displays it.
Why not server-to-client InvokeClient: the server would yield on the client. A malicious or slow client can never return (hang that server thread forever), return garbage, or error. If the player leaves mid-invoke, it errors. The server should never wait on a client for anything. A one-way RemoteEvent or replicated value gives the same UI update with no risk.
B14:
Teleport data (TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData, read with Player:GetJoinData) is passed through the client. The client can read and tamper with it, it is not guaranteed to arrive, and it has size limits. It is fine for non-authoritative things like the chosen map, party id, or a cosmetic loadout choice the match server re-validates. It must never be trusted for currency.
DataStores are authoritative, persistent and secure (server-only), but slower, rate-limited and eventually consistent across servers. The lobby must save (and release the session lock) before teleporting, and the match must load with session locking so it doesn't read stale data.
MemoryStores (HashMap/SortedMap) are fast, server-only and short-lived (TTL). They are good for handing off session state such as the loadout, match assignment or reservation keyed by userId, with an expiry.
Choice: keep coins in the DataStore (ProfileStore-style session lock: save on the lobby side, then load in the match). Put the loadout in a MemoryStore HashMap keyed by userId (or the DataStore too) and validate it against owned items in the match server. Use teleport data only for non-sensitive hints (match id), checked server-side.
B15:
One Script per instance (610 copies): every copy is a separate script VM context with its own connections. That means memory and startup cost, and an edit or bug fix has to be copied 610 times (or kept in sync via packages). Behaviour drifts, it's hard to profile, and copies get duplicated with the model and run even when streamed out.
Tag-driven: tag the instances (Door, Pickup, Turret) with CollectionService, and have one server Script or module per type (a component/system) handle all of them:
- For each tag: run setup on GetTagged(tag), connect GetInstanceAddedSignal(tag) for new or spawned instances, and connect GetInstanceRemovedSignal(tag) to disconnect and clean up (Maid/Janitor/Trove per instance).
- Configure each instance with Attributes (OpenTime, Damage, Respawn) instead of per-copy code.
- Turrets: one loop over the active turret set (a single Heartbeat) instead of 60 loops. Throttle or spatially cull them and only update turrets near players.
- Client-side visuals (door animation, pickup spin) use the same tag pattern in a client script. Under StreamingEnabled, the added and removed signals fire as instances stream in and out on the client, so code naturally handles streaming. The server holds the authoritative state (door open, pickup taken).
- Code lives in ServerScriptService/ReplicatedStorage modules, with one source of truth. Frameworks like a component library wrap this pattern.
B16:
Ownership: give the driver's client network ownership of the car (VehicleSeat.Occupant changed: car.PrimaryPart:SetNetworkOwner(player); on exit, return it to the server or nil). Client ownership makes driving feel responsive with no input latency. Server ownership would give laggy, rubber-banding steering.
Risk: the owner simulates the car's physics, and the server accepts whatever position and velocity they report. An exploiter can teleport, speed-hack, fly, fling other players with their car, or noclip, and the server sees it as legitimate physics.
The server must still validate:
- Sanity checks on position deltas and speed against the car's max speed (per heartbeat). Use checkpoint and lap order with timing (no skipping, minimum lap time). Out-of-bounds or under-map checks, and teleport detection. Reset or revoke ownership (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) or flag the player on a violation.
- All game outcomes: lap counting, finish times, rewards and collisions that damage others are decided on the server, never from client remotes.
- Ownership changes only when the seat is legitimately occupied. Don't let clients own unoccupied cars or other players' cars, and lock ownership with SetNetworkOwnershipAuto disabled. Use Server Authority mode where available.
B17:
Use UnreliableRemoteEvent for high-frequency, latest-value-wins data like aim and position. It has no ordering or retransmission, so packet loss doesn't stall the queue, and it is cheaper.
Constraints and handling:
- Delivery is unordered and lossy. Send absolute state (not deltas), include a sequence number or timestamp, and drop older packets on the receiver.
- Payload limit is about 900 bytes per event; bigger ones are dropped. Keep it tiny: quantize (aim as two 16-bit angles or a compressed vector, position via buffer), and use the buffer type to pack bytes.
- Never use it for important one-off events (fire, hit, purchase). Those stay on a reliable RemoteEvent.
- Reduce the rate. Send at 10-20 Hz or only when aim changes beyond a threshold, and interpolate on receivers. The character position already replicates through physics, so don't resend it. Batch multiple values into one event.
- Validate and rate-limit on the server like any remote (types, NaN, max rate, plausible angles).
- Rebroadcast to other clients, also unreliably, ideally only to nearby players.
B18:
Use Parallel Luau with Actors. Put the NPCs (or batches of them, for example 8-20 Actors each owning a group) under Actor instances, each with its own Script. In each Actor, connect RunService.Heartbeat with ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize()) to do the read-only, heavy work in parallel: raycasts (workspace:Raycast is parallel-safe), distance and path scoring, target selection. Then call task.synchronize() and apply the results serially: set CFrames or Humanoid:MoveTo, change properties, fire remotes.
Limitations to design around:
- In the parallel phase you can read most instances but cannot write most properties, create or destroy instances, or call many non-thread-safe APIs (check each API's thread safety). Writes happen only after synchronize, where they are serial again.
- Actors don't share Luau state: no shared tables or module state across Actors. Communicate with Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage or SharedTable (which costs synchronization). Each Actor's require gets its own module copy.
- Parallel work is worth it only for chunky work. Per-NPC actors with tiny jobs add overhead, so batch them. Schedule spreading (not every NPC every frame, staggered updates) often gives more.
- PathfindingService:ComputeAsync yields and isn't a parallel tool; compute paths less often.
- The thread count depends on the server's cores. Profile with the MicroProfiler.
B19:
Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled. The client then receives only the region around the player, which cuts join time and memory.
Settings: StreamingMinRadius around 64 (default) and StreamingTargetRadius around 1024 (default). Lower the target radius (256-512) for mobile-heavy or dense maps. StreamOutBehavior = Opportunistic, which frees memory as the player moves. StreamingIntegrityMode = Default or PauseOutsideLoadedArea, so players don't fall into unloaded areas. Use Model.ModelStreamingMode: Atomic for models that must load whole, Persistent only for a few always-needed things (sparingly), and PersistentPerPlayer where needed. Model LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh gives distant imposters.
Scripts that assumed everything is loaded:
- Client scripts must not index distant workspace paths directly. Use WaitForChild (with care), or better, CollectionService tag added and removed signals to attach behaviour when instances stream in and clean up when they stream out.
- Handle nil and stream-out (instances may disappear; disconnect).
- Before teleporting or moving the camera far, call player:RequestStreamAroundAsync(position).
- Keep authoritative logic on the server, where everything exists. Move client-required assets such as UI templates and VFX to ReplicatedStorage.
- Test with Studio's streaming emulation on low-memory devices.
B20:
Cause: each SetAsync is a write request. 80 players x 1 write per 5 seconds = 960 writes/min, but a server's write budget is about 60 + 10 x 80 = 860/min. Each key also allows only about 1 write per 6 seconds, so writing the same key every 5 seconds exceeds the per-key limit. Requests pile up in the throttle queue; once the queue is full (error 302, "request dropped, queue full"), saves are dropped and lost. SetAsync also blindly overwrites.
Better design:
- Keep data in a server-side session cache and mark it dirty on change.
- Autosave every 60-120 seconds (or longer), staggered across players (each on its own offset), and only if dirty.
- Save on PlayerRemoving and on BindToClose, plus right after important events (a purchase, via UpdateAsync).
- Use UpdateAsync with session locking (or ProfileStore). Check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before writing, and back off and retry on failure with exponential delay.
- Store one key per player (all their data in one table) rather than many keys. For high-frequency shared values, use MemoryStore or OrderedDataStore with less frequent writes.

B22:
Input Action System core instances:
1. InputContext: a group of actions that can be enabled or disabled together, with a Priority and Sink (block lower-priority contexts from receiving the same inputs).
2. InputAction: a named action with a Type (Bool, Direction1D, Direction2D, Direction3D, ViewportPosition). It exposes Pressed and Released (Bool), StateChanged(newValue), and GetState().
3. InputBinding: a child of an action that maps a physical input (KeyCode, gamepad buttons and axes, composite Up/Down/Left/Right keys for directions, or a UIButton for touch) to the action, with options like Scale, PressedThreshold and ResponseCurve.
Signalling: for a Bool action, when any binding crosses its press threshold, the action fires Pressed (and StateChanged(true)), and Released when it lets go. Scripts connect to these signals instead of polling raw input.
Menu precedence: create a "Menu" InputContext with a higher Priority than the default player-scripts context (the gameplay or character-controls context) and Sink = true. Enable it when the menu opens (context.Enabled = true), so its bindings (for example a gamepad confirm or back button) consume the input and lower contexts don't receive it. Disable it on close.
B23:
It is the UI Styling system (Studio's CSS-like styles for GuiObjects).
Main instances:
- StyleSheet: a container of rules, like a CSS file. Holds StyleRules and tokens (attributes).
- StyleRule: has a Selector string (class name such as "TextButton", tag ".Primary", name "#Title", state ":Hover", and descendant/child combinators) and property values set with SetProperty/SetProperties. Rules have a Priority, and nested StyleRules work like nested CSS.
- StyleLink: placed inside a ScreenGui or other UI root (or the DataModel). Its StyleSheet property points at a StyleSheet, which applies it to that UI tree.
- StyleDerive: lets one StyleSheet inherit or extend another (themes).
How styles reach UI: a StyleLink under a LayerCollector applies the linked sheet. Each GuiObject whose class, tags (CollectionService tags, written with a "." prefix in selectors) or name match a rule's Selector gets the rule's properties. A property set directly on an instance overrides the style. More specific or higher-priority rules win.
Tokens: define attributes on the StyleSheet (for example PrimaryColor = Color3, CornerRadius = UDim) and reference them in rule values with "$PrimaryColor". Changing the token changes every rule that uses it. Swapping in a derived sheet with different token values gives theming such as dark and light.
B24:
Roblox now requires a Facial Age Estimation check (a selfie video processed by a vendor, Persona, and deleted afterwards) to unlock chat. ID verification is an alternative for users 13+. Users who don't complete the check can't use chat.
Users are placed in age groups: under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20 and 21+. Chat is restricted to users in the same or adjacent age groups. For example, a 12-year-old can chat with users aged 9-15 but not with adults, and 21+ users can chat with 18+ users. Under-9s have chat off by default unless a parent enables it. Trusted Connections (verified as known in real life) allow chat across groups.
In games, use TextChatService (CanUserChatAsync / CanUsersChatAsync) and the built-in channels; the age gating is enforced through them. Custom chat systems must not bypass it. The rollout started in select countries in late 2025 and became global in early 2026.
